name: Tomas Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a stroke rehab ward, mostly nights, at the general hospital on the east side of town. At night it's turning people every two hours, checking swallows before anyone gets a drink, and calming people who wake up and can't find their words. I like seeing someone go from a hoist to a frame over six weeks. What wears me out is the body clock, and the families who ring at four in the morning because they can't sleep either.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what's your life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Amira, who's a teaching assistant at a primary school, and we're getting engaged properly next spring. We rent a two-bed flat above a bakery, which is lovely until five in the morning. We've got about five months saved, partly thanks to the night pay. I coach an under-twelves football team on Saturdays when the rota lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, not a miracle. At work the lads on the ward would probably joke that the robot isn't coming to do nights after all. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not one for opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe, and I think it was always going to be. Night shifts on a stroke ward aren't something a computer does. My worries are ordinary ones, like getting the deposit together and whether nights are wrecking my health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing nights for another two years to build the deposit, then go back to days. I'd keep using the drug-checking app now and then, the way most of us do. I'd put the night pay straight into savings, about three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned nights wrecking your health. How bad is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm twenty-seven and my knees ache like my dad's. I sleep five hours in the day if the bakery's quiet. It's fine for two more years, not for ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids you coach about jobs, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the boys to learn a proper trade or a profession with people in it. Nursing, plumbing, teaching, it doesn't matter. Work where you're needed in person is work that lasts.

I'd joke at work that no robot is coming to **do nights**.
think: He believes his **job is safe**, as computers don't nurse stroke patients overnight.
His worries are the **deposit** and the toll of **night shifts**.
do: Keep working **nights** for two more years, then return to days.
Save the **night pay**, about three hundred a month, toward a deposit.
Keep using the **drug-checking app** now and then.
feel: He feels **calm** and steady, with no real AI worry.
S0.quote: Night shifts on a stroke ward aren't something a computer does.
fieldNote: His calm rests on **five months** of savings and a hands-on job.
The real cost he names is **health**: aching knees at twenty-seven.
His advice to the boys shows a **traditional** belief in in-person work.

steps.text: Keep working nights on the stroke ward for two more years
Put about three hundred a month of night pay into the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible change and nurses should take what helps. At work I'd say let's see what it actually does before we panic. Most people would agree with that, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the paperwork side gets lighter and the ward gets thinner. If the computer writes the care plans and does the ordering, a manager will ask why we need five nurses on a night. I'm not worried for me, but I'd be one of fewer people doing more turns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools once the other nurses on the ward have tried them and say they're decent. I'd ask about the stroke specialist course, because specialists are harder to cut. And I'd keep the savings going and maybe hold off on the engagement party until we know the rota is stable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. The kind of feeling where you keep an eye on the noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be steering this change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospitals and the firms, honestly, not politicians. Government makes a mess when it tries to run things. But someone has to make sure the saving isn't just taking a nurse off nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the party. Would Amira be okay with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend Amira would roll her eyes, then agree, she's more careful than me. We'd still get engaged, just with a meal at her parents' instead of a hall. Her mum would probably prefer that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got to keep our heads and look after each other. At the mosque and at football I'd tell people to stick with family and save what they can. I'd probably sound calmer than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think 2028 takes the charts and plans but leaves me the turning and washing for three years. Then around 2031 I'd be thirty-one, maybe a new dad, and a robot could do my nights. Amira's job might go even sooner if AI can teach reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the engagement do entirely and put everything into savings, to get up to a year. I'd learn whatever system the ward runs on, so I'm the nurse who checks the robot rather than the one it replaces. And I'd look at a second skill with my hands, maybe the electrical course my cousin did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I've got three years and I don't know what to do with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad he was right to push me into a job with people. Then I'd tell him even that might not be enough. He drove a taxi for thirty years and saw the apps take it, so he'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound calmer than you are. What's the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say we'll be fine with family. Inside I'd be doing sums at three in the morning on the ward. Two incomes could become none in three years.

fieldNote: The **say-think gap** is plain: calm in public, sums at **3am** privately.

steps.text: Save toward a full year of household costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people stop arguing and get on with it. I'd tell the lads at work to pick a specialism now. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years changes a lot for us. Amira and I could get married and buy a small place before it hits. But I'd still think my nights are gone by 2034, when I'm thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the stroke specialist course in the next year and aim for a senior post that's more decisions than lifting. I'd buy a flat with a smaller mortgage than we'd planned. I'd use the AI tools more, since by then everyone would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's not the same as panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a senior post, if AGI does the thinking too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone still has to sign off and take the blame. A machine can't stand in front of a family and say sorry. I think the senior nurses last longest, even if there are fewer of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a smaller mortgage mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a flat instead of the little house by the park we liked. I'd rather be able to pay it on one wage. My uncle lost his house in the last recession and I've never forgotten it.

steps.text: Complete the stroke specialist course next year

Use the ward's AI tools daily as they arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and there's no excuse not to be ready. I'd say it at work and to the parents at football. People who plan will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes and forty when the robots are good, probably a senior nurse by then. The worry is more for my kids, if we have them, and what jobs are left for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to days in two years, do the specialist course, then aim for a ward sister post, the nurse who runs the ward, by my mid-thirties. We'd marry and buy a house on the normal timeline. I'd save for the kids' futures early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, mostly about the next generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What jobs would you point your kids to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know, and that bothers me. Maybe a trade, maybe something with people. I'd want them to work hard and stay close to family, whatever it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change how you'd coach the boys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd tell them school still matters, and so does character. Being someone people trust is something the football team teaches better than any app.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both of us could lose work within three years, just when we'd want to start a family. What would help is the hospital paying for specialist courses, not benefits. Give people a ladder and they'll climb it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the patients would want. A stroke patient who can't speak still squeezes your hand when you get their name right. I don't know if they'd squeeze a robot's.

headlineQuote: A stroke patient who can't speak still squeezes your hand when you get their name right.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old night nurse** on a stroke rehab ward, living with Amira.
He's **calm** about the mild pictures, believing hands-on night work is safe.
AGI by 2028 makes him **anxious**, with two incomes possibly gone in **three years**.
With more time he plans a **specialist course**, senior post and a cautious mortgage.
He favours **ladders over benefits** and trusts family, faith and hard work.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, since both household incomes could go together.
whatWouldHelp: He wants the hospital to pay for **specialist courses**, giving people a **ladder**.
